analysis.one_liner: Requires EPA to set strict disposal rules for toxic PFAS waste and bans burning it until then.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have banned burning toxic PFAS waste until the EPA writes strict disposal rules, died in a House subcommittee without a vote, no cosponsors, and no floor action.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have told the EPA to write rules for getting rid of PFAS — the "forever chemicals" used in nonstick and stain-resistant products and in firefighting foam — so they are destroyed rather than released into the air. It would have banned burning PFAS waste until those rules took effect, required incinerators to follow Clean Air Act limits including control of hydrogen fluoride, banned burning it near overburdened communities, and treated PFAS waste as hazardous waste for criminal penalty purposes.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live near incinerators and hazardous waste sites, especially the overburdened communities the bill defines and shields from PFAS burning, plus firefighters and military communities where PFAS firefighting foam is stockpiled and disposed of. Anyone exposed to PFAS through air near disposal sites would gain, because the chemicals do not break down and can accumulate in the body, with links in the record to adverse human health effects.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Residents near PFAS disposal and incineration sites

how_it_helps.text: Requires the EPA to write rules ensuring incineration of PFAS waste actually eliminates the chemicals, including from air emissions, rather than releasing them into nearby neighborhoods.
Bans incinerating PFAS or firefighting foam outright until the EPA's regulations take effect, closing the gap where the chemicals could keep being burned with no federal disposal standard.

Requires incinerators to meet Clean Air Act requirements including control of hydrogen fluoride, to be permitted waste facilities, and to store PFAS waste under hazardous-waste storage rules in the meantime.
Prohibits PFAS incineration in or near overburdened communities, the neighborhoods that typically host waste facilities and bear the health burden.
Treats PFAS waste as hazardous waste for criminal penalty purposes, so illegal dumping or burning carries real consequences.

analysis.who_pays: Companies that dispose of PFAS waste and firefighting foam — waste incineration operators and the industrial and military users of the foam — would bear the cost of the interim burning ban and of meeting stricter, permitted, emissions-controlled disposal once EPA rules arrive. Chemical manufacturers whose products generate the waste would face higher disposal costs as well. The EPA would bear the cost of writing the rules on a six-month deadline.
analysis.who_pays_short: PFAS waste handlers and chemical manufacturers

drawbacks.text: An immediate ban on burning PFAS waste, before alternatives are proven at scale, could leave stockpiles of firefighting foam and PFAS materials without a clear disposal route in the interim.

The bill demands that incineration 'eliminate' PFAS including air emissions — a standard that pushes the hard question of whether destruction is even achievable onto EPA rulemaking, which could mean litigation and delay rather than quick protection.

Stricter hazardous-waste handling, permitted facilities, and emissions controls would raise disposal costs for industrial users of PFAS and for firefighting foam stockpiles, some of which could pass through to consumers and public budgets.
It was a one-sponsor bill with zero cosponsors and was never marked up, so there is no record of how its costs and design questions would have been weighed by a committee.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential benefit — stopping the release of chemicals that never break down into the air of nearby communities — is real and durable, since PFAS exposure is essentially permanent for the people who absorb it. The main cost is a genuine practical one: an immediate burning ban with no certified alternative could complicate disposal of foam stockpiles in the short term. On balance the bill addressed a gap where hazardous waste was being burned with no federal standard at all, and the burden would fall on the waste handlers and manufacturers that created it.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Environment and Climate Change subcommittee, and no further action was ever taken before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Andy Levin introduced the PFAS Safe Disposal Act on July 16, 2021, requiring EPA regulations for PFAS disposal and an interim ban on incinerating the chemicals.
The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and, three days later, to its Subcommittee on Environment and Climate Change.
It drew no cosponsors and no subcommittee or committee action ever followed, leaving it to die when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: PFAS waste handlers, incineration operators, and the chemical manufacturers that generate PFAS waste avoided new disposal rules and the interim burning ban. Communities near incinerators gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: PFAS waste handlers and chemical makers

for.name: Andy Levin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its only sponsor.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Held the bill in committee without a markup or vote for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, and with zero cosponsors there is no record of where support or opposition would have fallen by party.

industries.industry: Hazardous waste handling and incineration operators
industries.note: The bill bans burning PFAS waste until EPA rules exist and then requires permitted facilities that meet Clean Air Act limits, raising the cost of a disposal business built on incineration. Its gain — cheap unregulated burning of PFAS — comes at the expense of air quality near disposal sites.

Producers of PFAS and of aqueous film-forming firefighting foam would face higher, more regulated disposal costs for the waste their products generate, and criminal hazardous-waste penalties for mishandling it.

industries.industry: Industrial and military users of PFAS firefighting foam
industries.note: These users would need to stockpile or find alternatives for foam they currently burn, an immediate cost, but would benefit from a clear legal disposal pathway once EPA rules are in place.
